title: $\Dctf=\Dbc$ for integral and rational coefficients
statement:
Fix a prime $\ell$, an algebraic closure $\Qlb$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, and a finite subextension $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ with valuation ring $\cO_E$. Use the commutative condensed coefficient rings [sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring], [sk-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed] and their pulled-back coefficient sheaves $\Lambda_X=p_X^*\Lambda$ [sk-def-sfb-pulled-back-coefficients]. Let $X$ be a qcqs scheme and $\Lambda\in\{\cO_E,E,\Qlb\}$ (including $\mathbf Z_\ell,\mathbf Q_\ell$). In this statement constructible means the finite constant local model convention [sk-def-sfb-constructible]: there is a finite constructible locally closed stratification on each stratum of which the module is pro-étale locally $\Lambda_U\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P$ for a finitely presented scalar module $P$. Use $\Dbc$, Tor amplitude and $\Dctf$ in the ordinary uncompleted derived category exactly as in [det-def-sfb-constructible-tor-amplitude]; no derived-completeness assumption is imposed. Then:

1. Every constructible $\Lambda_X$-module in degree zero has Tor amplitude in $[-1,0]$, and in $[0,0]$ if $\Lambda$ is a field.
2. For integers $a\leq b$, every $K\in\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ with cohomology in $[a,b]$ has Tor amplitude in $[a-1,b]$, and in $[a,b]$ if $\Lambda=E$ or $\Qlb$: for every degree-zero $\Lambda_X$-module sheaf $M$,
$$\mathcal H^r(K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda_X}M)=0\quad\text{for }r\notin[a-1,b],\quad\text{respectively }r\notin[a,b].$$
Consequently $\Dctf(X,\Lambda)=\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ as full subcategories of the same ordinary derived category.

For finite nonregular coefficients the condition is necessary. For $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$, the scalar module $\mathbf F_\ell=A/(\ell)$ has infinite projective dimension. The scalar complex $[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ is perfect [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex], while its two nonzero cohomology modules are $\mathbf F_\ell$, which is not perfect. These are also counterexamples as constant sheaves on $X=\operatorname{Spec}k$ for any separably closed field $k$: the constant residue module is constructible but has no finite Tor amplitude, whereas the two-term constant free complex has finite Tor amplitude. For every qcqs scheme $X$ and every finite commutative ring $A$ with discrete condensed structure, $\Dctf(X,A)$ is thick (triangulated and closed under direct summands), but it need not be stable under standard truncations.

proof.text: Put $c=-1$ for $\cO_E$ and $c=0$ for $E$ or $\Qlb$. Apply the uniform p-adic scalar-model theorem to every scheme $S$: every module with a finite constant local model has Tor amplitude $[c,0]$. Its integral case allows torsion scalar modules, and its algebraic-closure case uses the finite-subextension-valued condensed ring fixed here.

Apply finite-strata Tor dévissage with the common interval $[c,0]$ and the result of step 1 for every scheme $S$. Its constructibility predicate is precisely the finite constant local model convention fixed in the statement. Since $X$ is qcqs, it gives amplitude $[c,0]$ for every constructible module on $X$. The cited theorem permits arbitrary constructible locally closed strata: it uses an open–closed refinement, not an unsupported choice of an original open stratum. In the field cases enlarge $[0,0]$ to $[-1,0]$ by inclusion of intervals. This proves (1).

For $K$ as in (2), each $H^q(K)$ is constructible by the definition of $\Dbc$. Step 2 therefore gives its degree-zero complex amplitude $[c,0]$. Apply the cohomology Tor-interval theorem with cohomology interval $[a,b]$ and module interval $[c,0]$. Its conclusion is amplitude $[a+c,b]$, hence $[a-1,b]$ integrally and $[a,b]$ over a field. This includes the universal test against every degree-zero module, exactly as claimed.

Every $K\in\Dbc$ has some finite cohomology interval, so step 3 puts it in the finite-Tor subcategory. Conversely $\Dctf$ is defined as the full subcategory of $\Dbc$ consisting of finite-Tor objects. Thus their object predicates, and therefore their full subcategories and morphisms, agree.

For $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ and $t=\ell$, $t^2=0$ and $tr=0$ exactly when $r\in tA$: for an integer representative, $\ell^2\mid\ell r$ exactly when $\ell\mid r$. The periodic tensor theorem gives $\operatorname{Tor}^A_q(A/tA,A/tA)\cong A/tA=\mathbf F_\ell\ne0$ for every $q\geq0$. Thus there is no finite lower Tor bound. The existing scalar counterexample theorem also states infinite projective dimension and nonperfectness of this residue module, and perfectness of the two-term free complex. Directly, the latter complex has $H^{-1}=\ker(t)=tA\cong\mathbf F_\ell$ and $H^0=A/tA\cong\mathbf F_\ell$.

The finite-ring clause of the existing closure theorem gives thickness of $\Dctf(X,A)$ for every finite commutative discrete $A$ and qcqs $X$. On $\operatorname{Spec}k$ the constant square-zero example theorem supplies a constructible residue module with no finite Tor amplitude and a bounded constructible finite-Tor complex whose standard upper truncation has no finite Tor amplitude. For the two-term constant free complex $C=[A_X\xrightarrow{\ell}A_X]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ of step 5: its terms are the tensor unit of $\Mod(\Lambda_X)$, hence flat, and $\Mod(\Lambda_X)$ is a closed symmetric monoidal Grothendieck abelian category, so the bounded-above flat criterion makes $C$ K-flat. The relative derived tensor is computed by K-flat replacement, so $C\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda_X}N\simeq[N\xrightarrow{\ell}N]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ for every module $N$; thus $C$ has Tor amplitude $[-1,0]$. The failure of stability under standard truncations is the last conclusion of the example theorem, which proves the claim.
